title: Data-driven mechanistic models of morphology-controlled Ras oncogenic signaling
text:
Cell morphology drives oncogenic signaling in an entangled feedback interaction, regulating both intracellular
and environmental effects into cell behaviors such as survival and proliferation. Experimental approaches fail to
completely uncover the nonlinear mechanism between cell morphology and signaling because controlled
manipulation of morphology is often difficult and prone with side effects that turn experimental outcomes difficult
to interpret. Thus, I will develop a data-driven computational pipeline to study morphology-controlled signaling
mechanisms in the context of cancer cells.

title: Development and Application of Chemical Biology Approaches for Understanding Protein Arginylation
text:
While functional studies have identified arginylation as a regulatory post-translational modification on a few
proteins, modification sites and altered functions resulting from arginylation are largely unknown. This proposal
aims to unbiasedly unveil the arginylation sites in cardiovascular proteomes, elucidate the epigenetic and cardiac
development mechanisms of arginylation, explore the therapeutic potential of arginylation for targeted protein
degradation, and discover de-arginylation enzymes. These studies and technologies will provide a fundamental
basis to uncover the noncanonical functions of protein arginylation in cardiovascular development and disease.

title: The contribution of JNK signaling to development of EPR dysfunction in primary hypertension
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it identifies signaling alterations within the
dorsal root ganglion and potential therapeutic targets that will impact the clinical care of patients with
hypertension. This innovative proposal will explore the underlying mechanisms that drive exercise pressor
reflex dysfunction, specifically in primary hypertension. This project is aligned with The Surgeon General's
Call to Action to Control Hypertension “To provide targeted strategies that different sectors can take to
collectively improve hypertension control across the United States” and NIH’s mission “to foster
fundamental creative discoveries, innovative research strategies, and their applications as a basis for
ultimately protecting and improving health.”

title: Tissue Procurement Facility & Biospecimen
text: TISSUE PROCUREMENT FACILITY SHARED RESOURCE The Tissue Procurement Facility (TPF) is the main conduit for access to protocol driven tissue-based research. As part of the 2019 strategic plan, this SR was expanded and reorganized to provide additional services and with a more robust pipeline for faculty conducting this type of clinical research. The expansion of this resource led to enhanced services including: • More timely fresh tissue collection. TPF has developed a pipeline to collect fresh tissue for next-generation research focusing on single-cell and chip sequencing. The fresh tissue infrastructure requires significant collaboration between Surgical Pathology, Anatomic Pathology, TPF, and Clinical Protocol and Data Management (CPDM). For scRNA sequencing TPF has added an additional workflow to facilitate this methodology. • Tissue dissociation. TPF is equipped for single-cell dissociation to process tissue to single-cell for investigators that do not have the technology to do so and/or are investigating more robust experiments. • Ultrapure plasma processing. Ultra highspeed plasma purification for downstream cfDNA analysis. Ultrapure plasma will produce a significantly cleaner signal-to-noise ratio for investigators looking at cfDNA. TPFis led by an experienced faculty and staff. Dr. Calhoun is Director of Surgical Pathology and Anatomical Pathology at UNC and serves as Pathology Director. He works closely with the surgical liaison, co-leader HJ Kim to ensure responsible policies are in place for the procurement of research specimens following guidelines established by the UNC Hospitals. Amy Garratt serves as the Facility Director for the SR and its translational consenting and collection component. This is a well-managed resource with an operating budget of $1.0M. TPF requests $229,718 (21% of the total) for fiscal year 2020. LCCC members were more than 66% of the users in fiscal year 2019, virtually all other users were performing cancer research. The Facility procured, and distributed 46,091 specimens to support 154 different investigator-initiated studies.

title: Engineering Metal Ion-Immunity Crosstalk for Metalloimmunotherapy
text:
This research is relevant to public health because it aims to uncover how metal ions
interact with the immune system and develop innovative strategies to harness these
interactions for immune modulation. By advancing our understanding of metal ion-
immunity interactions and creating new delivery systems, this work has the potential to
lead to novel therapies for treating various immunological diseases, such as cancers and
inflammatory colon diseases.

title: Adult neurogenesis for improving urinary function after contusion spinal cord injury
text:
Spinal cord injury affects many patients and often leads to irreversible neuronal loss and autonomic
dysfunction. This proposed project will investigate a novel strategy for generating new neurons from resident
glial cells and their impact on bladder function following clinically relevant contusion injury. The results may
offer a regeneration-based therapy for patients with spinal cord injury.

title: MOCARB-RP1-Cd
text: ABSTRACT – RESEARCH PROJECT 1 (RP1) - Clostridioides difficile (Cd) Clostridioides difficile (Cd) infection (CDI) remains a major public health threat, causing almost 500,000 infections and 30,000 deaths annually in the U.S. Historically, CDI predominantly manifested as healthcare-associated (HA), typically developing within a week of acquiring new Cd during hospitalization. Over the last 15 years, interventions aimed at preventing these new acquisitions of Cd have resulted in significant reductions in HA-CDI. However, the incidence of community-associated (CA)-CDI has not decreased and now exceeds that of HA-CDI. This epidemiological shift aligns with a broader transition in pathogenesis, whereby most CDI cases, including HA-CDI, now result from pre-existing Cd colonization progressing to disease, a mechanism inadequately addressed by study models focused narrowly on new pathogen acquisition. Notably, CA-CDI differs from HA- CDI in several key ways: (1) CA-CDI involves a distinct prevalence of Cd strains that are adapted to community environments, (2) CA-CDI occurs against a less perturbed gut microbiome (GM) compared to HA-CDI, and (3) CA-CDI affects younger, healthier individuals with lower antimicrobial exposure than in HA-CDI. These differences highlight the need for a deeper understanding of CA-CDI, to uncover the genomic, GM, and host factors governing colonization-to-disease progression while developing models that reflect the ecological and clinical realities of modern CDI. The overarching hypothesis for this proposal is that Cd virulence, GM ecology, and GM-host interactions driving disease progression are more pronounced in CA than in HA cases, and these factors can be studied in-depth in GM-humanized gnotobiotic mouse models. Our central motivation is to derive fundamental new insights regarding CDI pathogenesis by integrating multi-omics analyses of a biospecimen repository of >30,000 stools from people with CA- and HA- Cd colonization and CDI. By leveraging our improved understanding of GM-pathobiont dynamics with innovative technologies, this proposal will pioneer development of novel diagnostic biomarkers, ecology-driven therapies, and management avenues to improve patient outcomes. To achieve this goal, we will: (1) Identify the Cd pan-genomic elements and Cd phages associated with CDI status from both CA and HA stools; (2) Ascertain Cd-GM-host interactions predictive of Cd colonization versus CDI in both CA and HA settings; and (3) Investigate post-antibiotic exposure CDI risk using defined GM- humanized mouse models. Our proposal is significant for elucidating the interactions between Cd, GM, and host factors that permit Cd colonization to progress to CA-CDI, the predominant mode of CDI pathogenesis today. Our approach is innovative as we employ multi-omics to analyze strains and stools across CA and HA cohorts, model and predict CDI via machine-learning, and validate our findings with a GM-humanized mouse model of Cd colonization-infection dynamics. This proposal is impactful, as it bridges fundamental research to translational solutions, resolving how strain variation, GM resilience, and host environment jointly govern disease development, premising precision ecology-driven therapies to reduce CDI and antibiotic resistance.

title: Fate Determinants of Basal-Squamous Pancreas Cancer
text:
Basal-squamous subclones within pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma are associated with worse prognosis and
therapy resistance, and it is not well understood what drives precancers and classical pancreatic ductal
adenocarcinoma to establish a basal-squamous identity. This proposal aims to determine whether the RNA
binding protein THO complex 3 (THOC3) is sufficient for the establishment of basal-squamous pancreas
cancer, and determine if THOC3 is necessary for the subsequent maintenance of its identity and growth. The
findings from this proposal will reveal the role of THOC3 in basal-squamous pancreas cancer formation and
maintenance, which may help address critical unmet needs for intervention and therapy development for the
highly resistant basal-squamous subtype, as well as further elucidate the role of THOC3 in oncogenesis.

title: Oral Dysplasia and Oral Cavity Cancer Risk in Dental and Medical Surveillance Settings Using a Chairside Chip-Based Cytopathology Tool
text:
Lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancers are a significant health problem afflicting approximately 530,000 people
globally every year. This multi-institution prospective longitudinal cohort study will assess for the first time the
performance of a point-of-care oral cytology tool (POCOCT) for its use in both secondary and tertiary care
settings, where high risk patients will be longitudinally monitored and their risk trajectory established over time
using personalized cellular image signatures. This effort has potential for more accurate oral lesion diagnosis
while improving patient survival and overall quality of life.

title: Excision Repair of Environmental Telomere Damage
text:
Telomere maintenance is essential for genome stability and the prevention of cancer and degenerative diseases.
The proposed research will examine how environmental genotoxic and oxidative stress cause accelerated
telomere shortening, and the pathways that preserve damaged telomeres. This project will reveal how various
forms of telomeric DNA damage impact telomere function, cellular function and organism health.

title: First murine animal model and adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy for MTATP6 mitochondrial diseases
text:
Mutations of the mitochondrial DNA-encoded ATPase 6 (MTATP6) gene lead to impaired mitochondrial ATP
synthesis, which results in a variety of neurological mitochondrial diseases. Allotopic expression of MTATP6 is
a plausible gene therapy approach for restoring mitochondrial dysfunction caused by MTATP6 mutations, while
to date it has only been tested in vitro due to the lack of an animal model. The proposed study aims to generate
the first MTATP6 targeting mouse model using a novel base editing technology, and develop an adeno-
associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy strategy for MTATP6 patients.

title: Multi-modal Approach to Understanding Airway Epithelial Development in Health and Asthma and its Modulation by Infant RSV Infection
text: PROJECT 1 – SUMMARY: Multi-modal Approach to Understanding Airway Epithelial Development in Health and Asthma and its Modulation by Infant RSV Infection The origin and clinical manifestations of asthma are tightly linked with dysfunctional physical, metabolic and functional barrier properties of airway epithelial cells (AEC). While leukocytes are also important in asthma pathogenesis, the airway epithelium is the primary site of respiratory viral infection, and many established asthma risk factors are exposures that interact with the airway epithelium. During the first year of life the airway epithelial barrier is continuing to develop, representing a critical time window of susceptibility to the effects of respiratory viruses that may contribute to the evolution of childhood asthma. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that there are distinct airway epithelial developmental endotypes present at birth that give rise to specific asthma phenotypes. These airway endotypes exhibit unique responses to environmental exposures such as RSV infection during infancy that contribute to asthma development. Developmental, metabolic and epigenetic programs drive abnormal, pre-asthmatic airway barrier changes and development of the early life epithelium that are key events in viral response and asthma inception. Approach: To test this hypothesis, we will use a human birth cohort study specifically designed during the current funding period to assess the longitudinal development of the airway epithelium, airway metabolism, DNA methylation, RSV infection and subsequent childhood asthma. Using an integrated approach we aim to identify clinically meaningful nasal mucosal endotypes, developmental pathways, metabolic changes and epigenetic alterations that will define normal and asthmatic airway epithelial cell biology and development and how respiratory viruses alter airway epithelial development to inform targeted prevention and treatments. We propose three aims focused on airway epithelial gene expression profiling, metabolic and epigenetic changes: Aim 1: Characterize the longitudinal biologic developmental pathways of the airway mucosa using scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq to define differences present at birth associated with subsequent wheeze and asthma risk, and whether development differs by resulting non-allergic and allergic asthma phenotypes. Aim 2: Identify the longitudinal changes in airway epithelial cell metabolism in infants that precede the development of asthma phenotypes in early childhood, and the specific metabolic pathways influenced by RSV infection that distinguish development of asthma phenotypes and endotypes. Aim 3: Determine the effect of early life RSV infection on airway epithelial DNA methylation (DNAm) and subsequent childhood asthma through identification of differentially methylated CpGs in longitudinal nasal airway epithelial sample cell types. Impact: The guiding principle of this program is to focus on clinically relevant research, and our program was designed specifically to address key gaps in our understanding of childhood asthma development so that translation of the work from these projects will elucidate the developmental heterogeneity of asthma which is critical to identifying biologic targets for prevention and treatment.

title: Center for Modeling Non-Coding Disease Variants: Resource and Service Core
text: RESOURCE AND SERVICE CORE Non-coding variants in disease have long been understudied due to the complexity of understanding their function, the lack of accessible tools to analyze them, and their tissue- and development-specific effects. The primary goal of the Resource and Service Section (RSS) Core is to bridge the Center for Modeling Non-Coding Disease Variants with the broader scientific community by providing a user-friendly platform for researchers to access cutting-edge resources for non-coding variant prioritization and disease modeling to alleviate the challenges associated with studying disease-associated non-coding variants. The RSS Core will collaborate closely with the Center's Bioinformatics Core to develop an intuitive web-based interface that allows researchers to input non-coding variants of interest and explore a range of outcomes, including conservation, tissue- and development-specific expression patterns, and functional screening results. This will lead to dedicated pages where researchers can directly order mouse models or human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) models tailored for their studies. The RSS Core will support the distribution of disease models to researchers by (1) importing mice from the Disease Modeling Core, conducting independent validation, and assessing their health status, (2) generating hPSC disease models and differentiating them into relevant cell types, (3) cryopreserving, storing, and cataloging each biological resource, (4) distributing these resources on a fee-for-service basis, and (5) coordinating with the Mutant Mouse Resource and Research Centers to ensure a seamless transition of models from the RSS to the broader research community.

title: Designer Cytokine Therapy of Hepatocellular Carcinoma
text:
PROJECT 4: NARRATIVE
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is associated with significant morbidity without a currently effective therapy.
We describe a novel molecular reagent, a Fusion Superkine, and an innovative delivery approach permitting
safe and efficient targeted systemic administration of therapeutic agents, including viruses, that employs
microbubbles and focused ultrasound to release therapeutic agents in the liver. The novel reagent and
innovative strategies we have developed, including an effective combinatorial regimen, have the capacity to
transform and enhance the clinical management of HCC.

title: AI-enabled mobile-based fundus imaging for diabetes screening
text: There is a need for lower-cost, easier to use sleek tools to help identify people with unknown type 2 diabetes and related eye damage called diabetic retinopathy (DR) in low resource settings or areas with less healthcare access. Photographs taken with mobile phone-based retinal (eye) cameras can be used as screening tool, based on a new artificial intelligence (AI) model to identify type 2 diabetes cases. In this study, the research team plans to develop and test the effectiveness, usability, cost, and acceptability of a mobile-phone-based retinal camera for type 2 diabetes and DR screening in both a small hospital-based study and a larger community outreach facility-based study in India, findings which could improve diabetes screening in the US and globally.

title: Project-002
text:
Project 2 will examine the role of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (Pparg) and Pparg-regulated 
pathways in urothelial homeostasis and regeneration in response to UTI. Specifically, we will examine how Pparg 
dependent transcription promotes urothelial differentiation and prevents squamous differentiation, a state 
associated with chronic injury in which the urothelium is replaced with an epithelial sheet similar to skin. 
Superficial cells are critical neuromodulators of the bladder stretch response. We hypothesize that their loss due 
to squamous metaplasia can lead or bladder disfunction, including chronic urgency and pain. In are proposed 
studies, we will leverage the Pparg pathway to identify molecular drivers that can restore endogenous cell types 
in the chronically injured urothelium.

title: Center for Systems Neurogenetics of Addiction
text:
RELEVANCE TO PUBLIC HEALTH (PROJECT NARRATIVE) OVERALL
The Center for Systems Neurogenetics of Addiction (CSNA) seeks to identify the biological relationships among
the stages and patterns of cocaine addiction and behaviors that predict drug abuse. To uncover these
relationships, we will make use of advanced mouse genetic tools that allow us to precisely and efficiently identify
the genes related to addiction, and computational methods that enable holistic study of genes, biological
molecules and behaviors. We will discover addiction-related genes, but we will also generate enabling resources
and services for the addiction research community to unravel the complexity of addiction risk.

title: INROADS Clinical Core
text: SUMMARY – Clinical Core PATHWAYS In the US, peanut allergy affects approximately 2.2% of children, 1.8% of adults, and can be potentially fatal, life-long and has adverse impacts on quality of life. There are recently FDA-approved options for desensitization treatment of peanut allergy. A commercial peanut oral immunotherapy (OIT) using low milligram doses is approved for ages 1-17 years and an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, omalizumab, is approved for those 1 year of age and older. These products were tested on children who react to a 100 mg dose of peanut or less (low threshold) during an oral food challenge (OFC) and aimed to provide protection from an accidental exposure. About 2/3 of those treated can ingest at least the equivalent of 2 peanut kernels, providing safety from small accidental ingestions. In our prior AADCRC grant period, we focused on children with a “higher threshold” peanut allergy, reacting to peanut doses >100 mg. We found that peanut OIT using inexpensive, store-purchased, home-measured peanut was 100% effective for desensitizing the children to meal-size amounts of peanut and was safe. Now, children with peanut allergy have multiple options for treatment, but the decisions for therapy are substantially based on the threshold of reactivity that can only be accurately determined through a medically supervised OFC. Importantly, an OFC is also the only means to accurately determine the therapeutic outcomes of treatment. The foundation of this Clinical Core is the clinical need to determine Precise Allergy THresholds With the purpose of Accurate immunotherapY Selection (PATHWAYS). Determination of threshold through an OFC allows personalized selection of therapy and monitoring of the outcome. The clinical need for these OFCs provides an opportunity to phenotype patients and monitor clinical outcomes while obtaining biosamples to address the overarching aims of this AADCRC program, Immunologic Trajectories of Peanut Desensitization (INROADS). The PATHWAYS Clinical Core will phenotype threshold and determine desensitization outcomes in children across the treatment pathways who are receiving clinically indicated OIT or omalizumab. It will support the goals of Research Projects 1 (MICRO- TRACK) and 2 (SPADE) in this AADCRC, which will provide crucial mechanistic insights regarding desensitization therapies. The PATHWAYS Clinical Core leverages existing treatment programs and highly experienced investigators and staff to ensure efficient enrollment, data collection, and data entry. We will build upon our stellar track record of successful biosampling in our prior AADCRC, where we obtained blood at 3 time points in 97.5% of 310 OFCs at 100% of the required volumes. The clinical data and biosamples from PATHWAYS will fuel the novel investigations in the 2 research projects. Interactions between the PATHWAYS Clinical Core and research projects and the management of samples and data will be coordinated and supported by this AADCRC’s Administrative Core and Data Stewardship Core. Our integrated program will enrich mechanistic understandings, advance personalized medicine, and identify new therapeutic targets.

title: Route 66 Endometrial Cancer SPORE
text: Endometrial cancer is more common than all other gynecologic cancers combined, and the incidence and death rates have both increased over the past 25 years. The work proposed will lead to both an improved understanding of endometrial cancer biology and new approaches to prevent and treat this disease. Additionally, this SPORE will expand the numbers of researchers dedicated to studying endometrial cancer.
